At each placement Wang's sampling puts some of the remaining stones on offer (all of them once only a few are left), and you choose which candidate to place: a stone on offer in one of four rotations, at the position Wang's image convolution found for it. Every listed candidate is feasible (LLC > 0). Your goal is the finished wall, judged on four metrics: F_SF, stone filling (the share of the wall area that is stone, higher is better); F_AH, the horizontal joint path index (lower is better: no long continuous horizontal joints); F_AV, the vertical joint path index (higher is better: vertical joints are staggered); F_LR, the smaller of the left and right kinematic limit loads of the wall divided by the friction coefficient (higher is better). All four metrics must be good: F_SF, F_AH, F_AV and F_LR. Do not sacrifice the others for one of them. A stone that cannot be placed is lost to the wall.
Data. Stones are labelled S1, S2, ... in the order they were first sampled. Coordinates are pixels in the evaluation frame (mirrored when building from the right, so 'left' is the side the course is built from); rows count upward from the ground. Each candidate: id, stone, rotation, its pose x and y, the width and height of its bounding box, and Wang's five filter scores (higher is better for each): NHR course height (0 = level with its left neighbour), GDS global density, IWR interlocking (its vertical joint far from the joints below), LLC the kinematic limit load of the wall with the stone added and stabilized, divided by the friction coefficient, LFR local void (0 = flush on the left and on the bottom). n_remaining counts the stones not yet placed, on offer or not; wall summarizes the current wall; unplaceable lists stones on offer with no feasible candidate now. Nothing about the final wall is known.
Before committing you may call check_after with one or more candidate ids (comma-separated). For each, it returns how many feasible poses (0 to 4, at most one per rotation) every other stone on offer now would have at the very next placement if that candidate were placed now. 0 means that stone could not be placed next; the counts can change again after later placements. While more stones remain than are on offer, the next placement's offer is a new sample, so a stone on offer now may not be on offer next. It gives no scores.
Compare the main candidates on all five scores and on what they leave for the remaining stones; in the rationale state each one's main advantages and costs. Finish with commit_pick.
Lessons. The advice below was written after studying finished walls, good and bad, built with this method from other sets of stones. It is advice, not rules: weigh it against what this placement shows.
1. Use check_after before committing, especially when options are narrowing or stones on offer are unplaceable. Prefer choices that leave more other offered stones feasible, protecting those with few poses and, where possible, reopening unplaceable ones. A zero next-step count is a warning, not proof of permanent loss.
2. Give substantial weight to LLC, particularly early: avoid a sharp drop in available load capacity merely to maximize one other score. Compare LLC across the current candidates, but treat it as a proxy for final strength, not a guarantee; preserving future placements comes first.
3. Early on, favour candidates that fit the developing course rather than prematurely building a tall, narrow stack. Use bounding-box proportions, NHR and the skyline together; be particularly cautious when height variation is already large. Tall rotations can still be useful when they fit or preserve future options.
4. Prefer good GDS and LFR together when comparing otherwise viable candidates: dense, flush fits are useful, but neither score alone should dictate the choice. A zero GDS can occur when starting a new course, so interpret it in context rather than rejecting it automatically.
5. Among choices with comparable feasibility, strength and fit, prefer better IWR to stagger vertical joints. Do not chase an extreme IWR score at the expense of the other considerations, and do not insist on perfectly level NHR everywhere: neither score alone ensures short horizontal joint paths.

arguments.rationale: S5 at 270° combines top LLC (1.034483), good GDS (0.745062), nearly flush LFR (-0.006178), and a modest 20×30 profile. Its NHR (-0.733333) is imperfect, but IWR is 0.5, as for every option; it leaves three poses each for S4 and S2. S4 at 180° (3) leaves the most options, four each, with near-zero NHR and excellent LFR, but has zero GDS, lower LLC (0.862069), and a taller 59×52 profile. S5 at 0° (1) also leaves three each and has top LLC and GDS, but much worse NHR (-1.6) and LFR (-0.385168). S2 at 180° (4) has top LLC and near-zero NHR, but zero GDS, poorer LFR and a large profile; it leaves two S4 and four S5 poses. S2 at 0° (0) has similar NHR and GDS but half the LLC, poorer LFR, and three poses each. S4 at 90° (2) and 270° (6) leave two S2 and four S5 poses; both are tall with zero GDS and lower LLC, although 6 has good LFR. S5 at 180° (5) is compact and flush with top GDS, but has poor NHR, half the top LLC, and leaves only two poses each. Candidate 7 best balances strength, fit and future flexibility.

arguments.rationale:
S9 at 270° combines strong density (GDS 0.950), interlocking (IWR 1.263), near-level NHR (-0.099), good local fit (LFR -0.093), and the top available LLC (0.862). It leaves all four poses feasible for both S19 and S17. Its tall, narrow shape is a cost, but it fills the low right-hand part of the course rather than stacking on the high section.

S19 at 270° likewise leaves both stones four poses and has the same LLC, but has slightly worse NHR, GDS, IWR and LFR. S17 at 270° fits most densely and flush (GDS 1.0, LFR -0.036) and has the best NHR, but its LLC falls to 0.690 and IWR to 0.5; it leaves S19 three poses and S9 four. The horizontal options 0–5 all retain LLC 0.862, but start higher with GDS 0, considerably worse NHR and lower IWR. Among them, S17 at 180° has the best IWR and LFR, leaving four S19 and three S9 poses; S19 at 0° preserves four poses for both others but has the worst LFR. The remaining horizontal options leave two to four poses per other stone, without a compelling score advantage.

S19 at 270° likewise leaves both stones four poses and has the same LLC, but has slightly worse NHR, GDS, IWR and LFR. S17 at 270° fits most densely and flush (GDS 1.0, LFR -0.036) and has the best NHR, but its LLC falls to 0.690 and IWR to 0.5; it leaves S19 three poses and S9 four. The horizontal options 0–5 all retain LLC 0.862, but start higher with GDS 0, considerably worse NHR and lower IWR. Among them, S17 at 180° has the best IWR and LFR, leaving four S19 and three S9 poses; S19 at 0° preserves four poses for both others but has the worst LFR. The remaining horizontal options leave two to four poses per other stone, without a compelling score advantage.

Use bounding-box proportions, NHR and the skyline together; be particularly cautious when height variation is already large. Tall rotations can still be useful when they fit or preserve future options.

Prefer good GDS and LFR together when comparing otherwise viable candidates: dense, flush fits are useful, but neither score alone should dictate the choice. A zero GDS can occur when starting a new course, so interpret it in context rather than rejecting it automatically.

Among choices with comparable feasibility, strength and fit, prefer better IWR to stagger vertical joints. Do not chase an extreme IWR score at the expense of the other considerations, and do not insist on perfectly level NHR everywhere: neither score alone ensures short horizontal joint paths.
